title: Reading the target menu
summary: How to read the target menu at a Sporting™ stand and a Compak® Sporting station: the order of traps, special targets and the type of each double.

body.html: The target menu is the board at the stand that tells the shooter what is coming: which traps, in what order, and what kind of doubles.

In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the menu lists the traps in shooting order and must name any special targets: 90 mm, 70 mm or 60 mm, battue or rabbit. Referees check beforehand that the traps match the menu. A layout gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles. The doubles may only use targets already shown as singles from the same stand, and the squad shoots the singles first.

Each double is marked with its type. On report: the second target leaves on the sound of the first shot. Simultaneous: both targets leave together. Rafale: two targets from the same trap, one after the other, in Sporting™ only. Menus look different from ground to ground, so read the words, not just the letters.

Example: on a line of 4 stands, one stand has only 3 traps, and 3 singles and 2 doubles are shot there. Its menu might read: singles A, B, C, then a simultaneous double A + B and a rafale C + C (the letters are traps). On this stand at least one double must be simultaneous or rafale: two doubles on report are not allowed (Chapter 2 · Doubles at a position with 3 machines).

In Compak® Sporting a menu is posted at each of the five stations. Each station has five targets, in one of three mixes: five singles; three singles and one double; or one single and two doubles. The singles may come from the traps in any order. All five stations have the same kind of double, and the stations are linked in a chain: the first target of each double is the last target shot at the previous station. For competitions FITASC offers 40 ready-made setting tables (plans of which traps are shot at each station).
Before stepping onto a Compak® Sporting station, many shooters say its menu quietly to themselves: “A, then F, then B, then C and E on report.” This can help them remember the order.

notes.html: Shooters really say “menu”, so keep the word when you translate.
Before your shooter steps up, read the menu aloud to them in their language, letter by letter: 'A, then F, then B, then the pair C and E on report.'

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Read the menu: on station three you have A, then F, then B, then the pair C and E on report.
phrases.meaning: Station 3: three singles, then a double on report; five targets in all.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Same traps, new menu — don't shoot from memory.
phrases.meaning: The order has changed since the last round.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Three singles, then a simo pair.
phrases.meaning: 'Simo' is short for a simultaneous double.

key_points.html: Read the menu before you step up: trap order, special targets, type of each double.
Sporting™ menu: traps in order plus special targets (90 mm, 70 mm or 60 mm, battue or rabbit).
A Sporting™ layout gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles; doubles use targets already shown as singles; singles first.
Doubles: on report, simultaneous, rafale (Sporting™ only).
Compak® Sporting: five targets per station, same double type on all stations, each double starts with the previous station's last target.

quiz.q: Which special targets must a Sporting™ menu show?

options.text: Only the colours of the targets
90 mm, 70 mm, 60 mm, battue or rabbit

quiz.explain: The menu must list the traps in order and any special target types.

quiz.q: In Compak® Sporting, with which target does each double start?

options.text: Always the target from trap A
A new target that was not shown before
The last target shot at the previous station
Any target the shooter chooses first

quiz.explain: The doubles chain across stations: each begins with the last target of the station before.

quiz.q: Which type of double exists only in Sporting™?
quiz.explain: Compak® Sporting doubles are on report or simultaneous; rafale is a Sporting™ double.
